## How they got there
Arsenal finished as runners-up after losing the final to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties, with the match ending 1-1 and a 3-4 penalty shootout result. Their path was defined by an exceptional profile where they recorded 3.0 points per game and a goal difference of 2.38 per game, both figures better than 100% of that season's group/league-phase teams. Additionally, they limited opponents to just 2.8 shots on target per game, a defensive metric that was superior to 97% of their peers in the same phase.

## Would the model have picked them?
The model would indeed have selected Arsenal, as they ranked second among all knockout teams with a probability of reaching the final at 25.6%. This likelihood is significantly higher than the base rate of 8.3%, which represents the chance for a random knockout team to reach the final. Although the model's expected stage was 1.52 on its scale, the nearest actual stage to this expectation is the semi-finals.

## Weak spots
Arsenal displayed clear areas where they beat fewer than half of that season's teams, specifically in fouls committed per game (13.9) and long passes as a percentage of total passes (11.4). They also recorded 450 passes per game, which was better than only 39% of their league-phase counterparts. These three statistics represent the team's weakest statistical areas during this campaign.

messages.content: You are a football performance analyst writing for a curious, data-literate reader. Use ONLY the facts provided. Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Better than this %' figures say how many teams the club beat on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where beating a team means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Write plain markdown without tables.
